strings.name: Martin Hellman
strings.summary: Martin Hellman’s work with Whitfield Diffie, alongside Ralph Merkle’s research, opened new ways to communicate securely without a previously shared secret. A longtime Stanford academic, he defended open cryptographic research and privacy, then applied risk analysis to nuclear deterrence and international security. His influence combines mathematical foundations with sustained attention to technological responsibility.

strings.highlights.highlight-1.title: Public-key cryptography
strings.highlights.highlight-1.text: Developed public-key ideas and key exchange with Diffie; Merkle’s work was another important foundation.
strings.highlights.highlight-2.title: Technology and peace
strings.highlights.highlight-2.text: Applied risk analysis to nuclear security and promoted research freedom and technology ethics.
strings.timeline.event-1.title: Discussed nuclear deterrence
strings.timeline.event-1.text: An interview connected systems thinking in cryptography with nuclear risk and cybersecurity.

strings.timeline.event-2.text: ACM named Hellman and Whitfield Diffie joint recipients for public-key cryptography.
strings.timeline.event-3.title: Book on relationships and peace
strings.timeline.event-3.text: Published A New Map for Relationships with his wife Dorothie.
strings.timeline.event-4.title: Stanford emeritus professor
strings.timeline.event-4.text: Left the regular faculty while continuing work on technological risk and public issues.
strings.timeline.event-5.title: Co-edited a US–Soviet dialogue
strings.timeline.event-5.text: Published Breakthrough with Anatoly Gromyko to explore peace in the nuclear age.
strings.timeline.event-6.title: New Directions in Cryptography
strings.timeline.event-6.text: Published with Diffie on public keys, digital signatures and a key-exchange method.
strings.timeline.event-7.title: Joined Stanford faculty
strings.timeline.event-7.text: Returned from MIT to research electrical engineering and cryptography at Stanford.
strings.timeline.event-8.title: PhD and MIT appointment
strings.timeline.event-8.text: Earned a Stanford electrical engineering doctorate and became an MIT assistant professor.
strings.timeline.event-9.title: Engineering bachelor’s degree
